groups.title: Data structures and command cost
groups.mechanism: Redis structures support different access patterns and command costs. In-memory storage does not make unbounded operations safe or remove network and allocation overhead.
groups.tradeOff: Compact modeling reduces work while oversized values and hot keys concentrate load.
groups.verify: Measure command latency and transferred bytes under realistic key cardinality and payload sizes.

questions.question: When should Redis be used?
questions.answer: When its supported structures and latency model fit caching, coordination or data-access needs with explicit durability and failure assumptions.

questions.question: How do strings, hashes, sets and sorted sets differ?
questions.answer: Strings hold scalar/binary values; hashes map fields; sets represent uniqueness; sorted sets associate members with ordered scores.

questions.question: Why should command complexity influence data modeling?
questions.answer: A command scanning a large structure can consume significant server execution time even when no disk read is involved.

questions.question: Why can one large Redis value degrade unrelated traffic?
questions.answer: Transfer, serialization and server work for the large value can dominate capacity and create latency for other operations.

questions.question: How would you model a leaderboard?
questions.answer: Use a sorted-set design with explicit score, tie and pagination semantics, then bound updates, retention and hot-key traffic.

groups.title: TTL and eviction
groups.mechanism: Expiration removes values according to time rules; eviction responds to memory pressure under the configured policy. Neither substitutes for a complete cache correctness contract.
groups.tradeOff: Memory bounds, freshness and hit rate compete and require separate settings.
groups.verify: Exercise expiration, memory pressure and key updates while checking origin load and missing-key handling.

questions.question: How do expiration and eviction differ?
questions.answer: Expiration follows a key's configured lifetime; eviction removes keys under a memory policy when memory pressure requires it.

questions.question: When should TTL jitter be used?
questions.answer: When many related keys would otherwise expire together and cause synchronized origin reloads; a single hot key still needs its own protection.

questions.question: Does updating a key always preserve its TTL?
questions.answer: No universal rule applies across commands and options. Verify the exact command's expiration behavior and use supported explicit options.

questions.question: Why is a missing cache key not proof the underlying record is absent?
questions.answer: The key may have expired, been evicted, never loaded or become unavailable; consult the authoritative data under the cache policy.

questions.question: How would you select an eviction policy?
questions.answer: Use workload locality, key lifetime requirements and memory limits, then test both useful hit rate and safe behavior when entries disappear.

groups.title: Cache-aside and invalidation
groups.mechanism: Cache-aside separates lookup, origin load and cache fill. Concurrent updates can race with loaders, while invalidation failures can retain obsolete representations.
groups.tradeOff: Lower origin load comes with stale-data and coordination obligations.
groups.verify: Pause a loader, commit an update and resume the old loader to test stale repopulation.

questions.question: What is cache-aside?
questions.answer: Application-controlled cache lookup followed by authoritative loading on miss and storing the result under an explicit freshness policy.

questions.question: When is negative caching useful?
questions.answer: For repeated confirmed absence with a short appropriate lifetime, while distinguishing missing data from failed or unauthorized lookups.

questions.question: Why can deleting a key before database commit leave stale data?
questions.answer: Another reader can reload the old committed state before the write completes and repopulate the cache.

questions.question: Why must tenant and currency sometimes be part of a key?
questions.answer: They can change the result's meaning; omitting them can mix distinct prices or expose another tenant's data.

questions.question: How would you prevent stale loaders from overwriting fresh values?
questions.answer: Use a deliberate version or generation protocol, controlled invalidation/reconciliation or an accepted bounded-staleness design, tested against the actual race.

groups.title: Pipelining and atomicity
groups.mechanism: Pipelining reduces network round trips but does not turn several commands into one isolated transaction. MULTI/EXEC and WATCH have specific execution and conflict semantics.
groups.tradeOff: Batching improves throughput while larger batches increase outstanding memory and latency.
groups.verify: Interleave another client with pipelined or transactional updates and inspect actual visible states.

questions.question: What does Redis pipelining optimize?
questions.answer: It sends multiple commands without waiting for each response individually, reducing round-trip overhead rather than changing each command's semantics.

questions.question: How does MULTI/EXEC differ from pipelining?
questions.answer: It queues commands for transactional execution under Redis's contract; pipelining alone provides no equivalent multi-command isolation.

questions.question: What does WATCH support?
questions.answer: Optimistic conflict detection on watched keys so a transaction can be aborted if relevant changes occur before execution.

questions.question: Why is Redis transaction error handling not ordinary SQL rollback?
questions.answer: Redis does not generally undo earlier command effects when a queued command encounters an execution-time error; understand the documented error categories.

questions.question: How would you implement a safe conditional multi-command update?
questions.answer: Use the appropriate supported atomic operation, WATCH retry protocol or bounded script/function, then test concurrent conflicts and command failures.

groups.title: Scripts and bounded execution
groups.mechanism: Scripts execute under Redis's atomic execution model but must remain bounded. Blocking other operations and cross-slot constraints matter operationally.
groups.tradeOff: Server-side logic reduces round trips while increasing the blast radius of slow or faulty code.
groups.verify: Use small adversarial inputs and inspect latency, key declaration and failure semantics.

questions.question: When is a Lua script useful in Redis?
questions.answer: When a bounded multi-step key operation needs atomic execution and cannot be expressed adequately with a simpler supported command.

questions.question: Does script atomicity imply automatic rollback on every error?
questions.answer: No. Atomic execution prevents interleaving, but runtime errors do not universally restore effects of commands already performed.

questions.question: Why must scripts declare and use supported key arguments?
questions.answer: Correct key identification is important for execution, routing and cluster constraints; avoid arbitrary hidden key construction.

questions.question: Why is scanning an unbounded dataset inside a script dangerous?
questions.answer: It can monopolize server execution and delay unrelated traffic, turning one request into a broader latency incident.

questions.question: How would you review a production Redis script?
questions.answer: Check bounded work, numeric/argument validation, key scope, cluster compatibility and partial effects on failure using the actual Redis version.

groups.title: Distributed locks and fencing
groups.mechanism: A lease controls temporary ownership under assumptions about time, failure and recovery. A stale holder can keep running after expiry, so downstream enforcement may be needed.
groups.tradeOff: Coordination reduces overlap but can become another availability dependency.
groups.verify: Pause a holder past expiry, start another and verify stale effects are rejected where required.

questions.question: Why use a unique token for a Redis lock owner?
questions.answer: Release must confirm the caller still owns that lease, preventing an old holder from deleting a newer holder's lock.

questions.question: Why is SET NX with expiry not a complete business correctness proof?
questions.answer: The owner can pause, the lease can expire and another owner can start while the first continues executing.

questions.question: What is a fencing token?
questions.answer: A monotonically ordered ownership marker checked by the protected storage or service so stale owners cannot apply effects.

questions.question: Why is deleting a lock key unconditionally unsafe?
questions.answer: A delayed former owner can remove the current owner's lock after its own lease expired.

questions.question: How would you decide whether Redis locking is appropriate?
questions.answer: State the protected invariant, failure and failover assumptions, and whether stale effects can be rejected; prefer database constraints for invariants they can enforce directly.

groups.title: Replication and durability
groups.mechanism: Replication, persistence and failover have distinct guarantees. Acknowledged writes can still have loss or visibility implications under configured failure modes.
groups.tradeOff: Lower latency can trade against durability and recovery complexity.
groups.verify: Crash and fail over under realistic persistence settings, then reconcile acknowledged operations.

questions.question: How do RDB snapshots and AOF differ?
questions.answer: Snapshots persist selected dataset points; append-only persistence records write operations under configured policies, with different recovery and resource trade-offs.

questions.question: Does Redis replication make every acknowledged write lossless?
questions.answer: No universal guarantee follows; replication and failover timing plus persistence configuration determine potential loss.

questions.question: Why can replica reads be stale?
questions.answer: Replication can lag, so the replica may not yet contain the primary's latest acknowledged state.

questions.question: What does WAIT fail to guarantee universally?
questions.answer: Replica acknowledgment does not by itself turn Redis into a strongly consistent system or eliminate every failover data-loss scenario.

questions.question: How would you use Redis for important durable state?
questions.answer: Evaluate required loss tolerance against actual persistence and failover behavior, retain recovery evidence and use a more suitable authority when guarantees do not fit.

groups.title: Cluster distribution and hot keys
groups.mechanism: Redis Cluster distributes keys through slots; a single hot key remains concentrated. Multi-key operations need compatible key placement under cluster rules.
groups.tradeOff: Sharding spreads independent keys but complicates cross-key atomicity and client behavior.
groups.verify: Test slot movement, redirects and one extremely hot key separately from uniform traffic.

questions.question: What does Redis Cluster distribute?
questions.answer: Key slots across nodes, allowing different keys to be served by different shard owners under cluster routing rules.

questions.question: When are hash tags useful?
questions.answer: When related keys deliberately need the same slot for supported multi-key operations, while avoiding excessive concentration.

questions.question: Why can a multi-key command fail with cross-slot keys?
questions.answer: Its atomic or routing contract may require all keys in one slot, which the chosen key names do not satisfy.

questions.question: Why does adding shards not solve a single hot key automatically?
questions.answer: One key still maps to one slot owner; use appropriate local caching, replication of immutable representations or redesigned access patterns.

questions.question: How would you validate a cluster-aware client?
questions.answer: Exercise redirects, failover, slot migration, connection limits and safe retries, including ambiguous outcomes for side-effecting commands.

groups.title: Streams and delivery
groups.mechanism: Streams provide persisted entries and consumer-group progress under their configured retention and acknowledgment model. Pub/Sub has different delivery and replay behavior.
groups.tradeOff: Durable replay aids recovery while requiring pending-work and retention ownership.
groups.verify: Crash after applying an effect but before acknowledgment and inspect pending reclamation.

questions.question: How do Redis Streams differ from Pub/Sub?
questions.answer: Streams retain entries for supported reading/replay and consumer-group workflows; ordinary Pub/Sub is not a durable replay queue.

questions.question: What does a stream consumer acknowledgment represent?
questions.answer: Progress in the consumer-group delivery model; it does not atomically commit an external database effect.

questions.question: Why must pending messages be monitored?
questions.answer: A consumer can disappear or fail without acknowledging, leaving work requiring controlled recovery or reassignment.

questions.question: Why can aggressive trimming harm recovery?
questions.answer: Entries needed by lagging or recovering consumers can be removed before they are safely processed.

questions.question: How would you build a reliable stream consumer?
questions.answer: Use durable operation identity, bounded pending work, intentional acknowledgment timing and tested recovery for crashes, poison messages and retention limits.

groups.title: Security and operations
groups.mechanism: Redis access needs explicit network restriction, authentication/authorization and transport protection where required. Diagnostics must avoid leaking data or blocking the server.
groups.tradeOff: Convenient administrative commands can impose substantial production load or expose payloads.
groups.verify: Test denied commands, connection exhaustion and diagnostic overhead with representative data.

questions.question: Why should Redis not be exposed directly to arbitrary clients?
questions.answer: Its data and administrative command surface can permit disclosure, modification or resource exhaustion without appropriate access boundaries.

questions.question: When should ACLs be used?
questions.answer: To restrict principals to required command and key scopes under supported Redis authorization capabilities, alongside network and transport controls.

questions.question: Why prefer SCAN to KEYS for many production inventories?
questions.answer: SCAN offers incremental traversal, though results and iteration guarantees still require correct handling; KEYS can impose a large blocking traversal.

questions.question: Why can a connection pool become the bottleneck before Redis CPU?
questions.answer: Clients may wait for connections or hold them too long, consuming deadlines even when server execution capacity is available.

questions.question: How would you diagnose Redis latency safely?
questions.answer: Correlate client acquisition, network, payload size, slow commands, memory and server latency evidence using bounded diagnostics and restricted data access.
